Everything else is explanation.\n29\t\n30\t---\n31\t\n32\t## 1. Objective\n33\t\n34\t> **A static website that accepts a file from the user and turns it into a visual\n35\t> transmission on screen, which a second device running the same page receives through\n36\t> its camera and reconstructs into the original file.**\n37\t>\n38\t> **It must handle large files — on the order of multiple gigabytes.**\n39\t\n40\t- **Static.** No backend. Files on a CDN, works offline, auditable once and trusted\n41\t  thereafter. There is nowhere to upload anything *to*.\n42\t- **Same page, both roles.** One deployment; the user picks sender or receiver.\n43\t- **Screen → camera is the only channel.** Strictly one-way, lossy, low-bandwidth.\n44\t- **Multi-gigabyte.** The requirement that most shapes the architecture (§3).\n45\t\n46\t### 1.1 The honest framing of \"multiple gigabytes\"\n47\t\n48\tMulti-GB support is an **architectural** requirement, not a performance promise. The\n49\tdesign must never *forbid* a large file, run out of memory, or blow up super-linearly.\n50\tBut the channel's physics are what they are:\n51\t\n52\t| File size | Stage 1 (30 KB/s) | Stage 2 (60 KB/s) | Stage 3 (106 KB/s) |\n53\t|---|---|---|---|\n54\t| 100 MB | 57 min | 28 min | 16 min |\n55\t| **1 GB** | **9.7 h** | **4.9 h** | **2.7 h** |\n56\t| **10 GB** | **4.0 days** | **2.0 days** | **27.5 h** |\n57\t| 100 GB | 40.5 days | 20.2 days | 11.4 days |\n58\t| 1 TB | 414 days | 207 days | 117 days |\n59\t\n60\t> All figures are **user-visible file bytes**, not wire bytes. See §13.2 — with\n61\t> compression on, the two differ by 3–10× on compressible input, and quoting the wrong\n62\t> one would overstate throughput.\n63\t\n64\t**Gigabytes are hours-to-days. Terabytes are months.** Three design consequences follow,\n65\tand they are as load-bearing as any coding decision:\n66\t\n67\t1. **Resume is not optional** (D22). Nobody holds a phone for 27 hours.\n68\t2. **Neither side may hold the file in memory** (D20).\n69\t3. **The app states the estimated time before the user commits** (D23). Letting someone\n70\t   start a 40-day transfer without saying so is a product failure, not an edge case.\n71\t\n72\t---\n73\t\n74\t## 2. Glossary\n75\t\n76\tSeveral of these words are overloaded in the surrounding literature, and two of them\n77\t(*block*, *frame*) mean different things in different research documents. Within this\n78\tplan they mean exactly this:\n79\t\n80\t| Term | Meaning here |\n81\t|---|---|\n82\t| **Fragment** | The atomic unit the fountain code operates over. Fixed length **L** for the whole session (D15). |\n83\t| **K** | Number of fragments in one block. Derived as `blockSize / L`; never transmitted (D7). |\n84\t| **Block** | A contiguous slice of the (possibly compressed) payload, cut into K fragments and fountain-coded independently. **Always means this** — never \"fountain block\" or \"QR block\". |\n85\t| **Packet** | One fountain-coded symbol: 13-byte header + L payload bytes. The unit a tile carries. |\n86\t| **Tile** | One QR symbol on screen. Carries exactly one packet. |\n87\t| **Frame** | One displayed image, containing a grid of tiles. **Never** a video frame — those are *camera frames*. |\n88\t| **Camera frame** | One image captured by the receiver's camera. |\n89\t| **Beacon** | A special **packet** carrying file-level metadata instead of payload. Beacon packets are encoded into tiles and mixed into display frames by the frame mixer (D17, §7.2). |\n90\t| **Profile** | A modulation configuration: QR version, module pixel size, tile count. Several coexist per frame (D16). |\n91\t| **Dwell** | How many packets the sender emits for one block before advancing (§8.1). |\n92\t| **Screen px** | A pixel on the *sender's display*. What the renderer controls. |\n93\t| **Camera px** | A pixel in the *receiver's captured frame*. What the decoder actually sees. |\n94\t| **px/module** | **Always CAMERA px per module unless explicitly written \"screen px/module\".** The 4 px/module decode cliff is a *camera*-pixel figure. Conflating the two put every S2/S3 optical run below the cliff — see `../notes/spike-results.md` §S3. |\n95\t| **Magnification** | `camera_px_per_module = screen_px_per_module × M`, where `M` = (capture width across the code region) / (code region width in screen px). A 1920-px-wide landscape code region filling a 1080-px-wide portrait capture gives **M = 0.5625**, so 4 screen px/module is only **2.25 camera px/module**. |\n96\t| **Erasure** | A packet that did not arrive or failed validation. Never a corrupted packet — those are discarded, not used. |\n97\t| **Stage** | A modulation generation: 1 = tiled mono QR, 2 = + RGB tripling, 3 = custom grid codec. |\n98\t| **Pass** | One complete traversal of every block by the sender. |\n99\t\n100\t---\n101\t\n102\t## 3. What multi-gigabyte breaks, and the fix\n103\t\n104\tFour assumptions in the pre-multi-GB design do not survive contact with a 4 GB file.\n105\t\n106\t### 3.1 The fountain decoder does not scale — in TIME, not memory\n107\t\n108\tThis is the correction the plan review surfaced, and it matters because the first\n109\tversion of this section got it half right.\n110\t\n111\tD5 chose an LT code with a **Gaussian elimination** decoder, verified at\n112\t[`sim/`](../research/sim/). GE costs O(K²) in *memory* and O(K³) in *bit operations*.\n113\tThe original block-layer decision sized K from the memory term alone and concluded 4 MB\n114\tblocks (K = 16,384) were fine because the coefficient matrix is only 32 MB.\n115\t\n116\t**The memory term was never the binding constraint. Time is.**\n117\t\n118\tEach arriving packet is reduced against up to `rank` stored pivot rows; each row\n119\toperation XORs the coefficient mask (K/8 bytes) *and* the payload (L bytes). Reaching\n120\tfull rank costs `W = 2 · (K²/2) · (K/8 + L) = K² · (K/8 + L)` bytes of memory traffic,\n121\tand the block only lasts `K·L / R` seconds at wire rate R — so the decoder must\n122\t**sustain**:\n123\t\n124\t```\n125\trequired = W / (K·L/R) = K · (K/8 + L) · R / L    bytes/sec\n126\t```\n127\t\n128\t> The leading factor is **1, not 2** — the 2 and the /2 in `W` cancel. A previous\n129\t> revision of this section printed `2 · K · (K/8 + L) · R / L` and was 2× too\n130\t> pessimistic in every derived figure. Gate **G7** now diffs this section against the\n131\t> model so the class of error cannot recur.\n132\t\n133\tAll figures below are emitted by\n134\t[`sim/ge_cost_model.py`](../research/sim/ge_cost_model.py) — this section quotes the\n135\tmodel rather than reasoning beside it. **All rows at Stage 1 (R = 30 KB/s)**, so they\n136\tare comparable:\n137\t\n138\t| K | L | Block | Matrix | Work/block | Sustained need | |\n139\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n140\t| 1,000 | 1260 | 1.2 MB | 122.1 KB | 1.3 GB | 33.8 MB/s | research baseline |\n141\t| 1,500 | 1260 | 1.8 MB | 274.7 KB | 3.0 GB | 52.9 MB/s | research partitioning ceiling |\n142\t| 4,000 | 1260 | 4.8 MB | 1.9 MB | 26.2 GB | 171.6 MB/s | research called this **\"too slow\"** |\n143\t| **16,384** | **256** | **4.0 MB** | **32.0 MB** | **576.0 GB** | **4.5 GB/s** | **23× over budget** |\n144\t\n145\tThe plan's own evidence base\n146\t([`fountain-codes-and-protocol.md`](../research/fountain-codes-and-protocol.md) §2.6)\n147\tstates: *\"Cost scales as K², so it must be bounded. At K = 4000 the decode work is ~16×\n148\tthat of K = 1000 (~6 GB of XOR) — too slow\"* and recommends *\"source-block partitioning\n149\tabove K ≈ 1500\"*. **K = 16,384 was 11× past that ceiling.**\n150\t\n151\tIt was worse than a simple overshoot: shrinking L to 256 B to fit small tiles made the\n152\tmask term (K/8 = 2048 B) dominate the payload term (256 B) by 8×, so the decode problem\n153\tgot *harder* as a side effect of a decision made for a different reason.\n154\t\n155\t**Two further findings from the model:**\n156\t\n157\t- **A faster wire rate makes decode harder** — same work, less time to do it. So K MUST\n158\t  be sized for the *fastest* stage we intend to reach (Stage 3, 106 KB/s), not the\n159\t  slowest. This is counterintuitive and is why the original error was easy to make.\n160\t- **The sender's cost was unbudgeted too.** §6.3.1 counted QR encode and render but not\n161\t  the fountain XOR. At uncapped harmonic degree and K = 16,384 that is 398 KB of XOR\n162\t  per packet — **91.8 MB/s** at the old 225 packets/s (1 packet/tile), or **183.6 MB/s**\n163\t  at the adopted 450 packets/s (2 packets/tile at R2 nominal), on top of everything\n164\t  else. Hence D25.\n165\t\n166\t**Fix — D19:** K = **768**, L = **256 B**, block = **192.0 KB**.\n167\t\n168\t| | Was | Now |\n169\t|---|---|---|\n170\t| K | 16,384 | **768** |\n171\t| L | 256 B | **256 B** (unchanged — see §3.1.1) |\n172\t| Block | 4 MB | **192.0 KB** |\n173\t| GE matrix | 32.0 MB | **72.0 KB** |\n174\t| Block-layer working set | ~36 MB (claimed) | **264.0 KB** |\n175\t| Sustained need @ Stage 3 | 14.9 GB/s | **114.6 MB/s** |\n176\t\n177\t*Both \"sustained need\" figures are at Stage 3, so they compare like with like. The\n178\t4.5 GB/s in the table above is the same design at Stage 1.*\n179\t\n180\t**K_max at Stage 3 is 1152.** We adopt **768** deliberately below the ceiling —\n181\tD26 requires the sender to assume the weaker receiver, and the 200 MB/s budget is\n182\titself an unmeasured estimate (§18 R1). Margin at Stage 3: **1.74×**.\n183\t\n184\t| K | Block | Stage 1 | Stage 2 | Stage 3 | |\n185\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n186\t| 512 | 128.0 KB | 19.7 MB/s | 39.3 MB/s | 69.5 MB/s | 2.88× margin |\n187\t| **768** | **192.0 KB** | **32.4 MB/s** | **64.9 MB/s** | **114.6 MB/s** | **adopted, 1.74× margin** |\n188\t| 1024 | 256.0 KB | 47.2 MB/s | 94.4 MB/s | 166.7 MB/s | 1.20× margin |\n189\t| 1152 | 288.0 KB | 55.3 MB/s | 110.6 MB/s | 195.4 MB/s | 1.02× — the ceiling |\n190\t| 1536 | 384.0 KB | 82.6 MB/s | 165.2 MB/s | 291.8 MB/s | 1.5× **over** at Stage 3 |\n191\t\n192\t### 3.1.1 L is set by the *conservative* ladder rung, not the nominal one\n193\t\n194\tA revision of this plan briefly set L = 507 B (\"one packet per v15 tile\") and broke\n195\tD16's ladder. D15's source note states the governing rule plainly: **pick L to fit the\n196\tsmallest tile any profile would use.** At L = 507 the packet is 520 B and the\n197\tconservative rung, v10-L, holds **271 B** — so it could carry **zero** packets, only\n198\tbeacons. That destroys the ladder's one load-bearing property: *a mis-guessed profile\n199\tyields zero; a ladder always yields something.*\n200\t\n201\t**Rungs are therefore defined by packet count, with the QR version chosen to fit** —\n202\tnot the reverse. At L = 256 B, packet = 13 + 256 = **269 B**:\n203\t\n204\t| Rung | Packets | Needs | QR version | Capacity | Waste |\n205\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n206\t| R1 conservative | 1 | 269 B | v10-L | 271 B | 2 B |\n207\t| R2 nominal | 2 | 538 B | v16-L | 586 B | 48 B |\n208\t| R3 aggressive | 3 | 807 B | v20-L | 858 B | 51 B |\n209\t| R4 (probe only) | 4 | 1076 B | v23-L | 1091 B | 15 B |\n210\t\n211\tWaste stays ≤ 51 B on every rung. The pressure that motivated raising L has also\n212\tgone: at K = 768 the mask term is K/8 = 96 B against a 256 B payload (27%), not the\n213\t8× dominance that made L = 256 pathological at K = 16,384.\n214\t\n215\t**A rung MUST carry a whole number of packets.** Partial packets across tiles would\n216\tcouple tiles together and destroy the independence D1 depends on.\n217\t\n218\t### 3.2 Neither side can hold the file in memory\n219\t\n220\tA multi-GB `Uint8Array` is not allocatable (Chrome's `ArrayBuffer` ceiling is ~2 GB;\n221\tSafari's is lower), and would get a phone tab killed regardless.\n222\t\n223\t**Fix — D20:** stream both ends. `File.slice()` on the sender, OPFS on the receiver, one\n224\tblock resident at a time.\n225\t\n226\t### 3.3 The whole-file hash cannot be computed in one pass\n227\t\n228\t`crypto.subtle.digest` has **no streaming API** — it takes one buffer.\n229\t\n230\t**Fix:** per-block hashes (cheap, and they let each block be written as it completes,\n231\tthen verified retroactively once the manifest arrives) plus an optional whole-file hash\n232\tfrom an incremental WASM hasher. See §7.4 for how this interacts with `streamId`.\n233\t\n234\t### 3.4 Miss recovery gets expensive as blocks multiply\n235\t\n236\tAt 192 KB per block a 4 GB file is ~21,800 blocks. Sequential dwell means a block missed\n237\ton pass 1 waits for pass 2 — hours. **Fix:** the repair code (§8.2), which makes recovery\n238\tsub-minute and is why smaller blocks are affordable.\n239\t\n240\t---\n241\t\n242\t## 4. Decisions\n243\t\n244\t| # | Decision | Rationale | Source |\n245\t|---|---|---|---|\n246\t| **D19** | **Block layer: independent 192.0 KB blocks, K = 768, L = 256 B** | GE cost is bound by *time*, not memory (§3.1). K = 768 keeps pace at Stage 3's 106 KB/s (114.6 MB/s needed, **1.74x margin**) within a conservative 200 MB/s phone-JS budget; matrix is 72.0 KB and the block-layer working set 264.0 KB, flat regardless of file size. K_max is 1152; 768 is deliberate conservatism per D26. **L is set by the conservative ladder rung** (S3.1.1), not the nominal one. What RFC 6330 calls source blocks. | §3.1, `sim/ge_cost_model.py` |\n247\t| **D27** | **The receiver duty-cycles BLOCKS under receiver-side thermal pressure; multi-GB is framed as multi-session** | Measured: a Pixel 6 hit 70 °C and its throttling threshold in **20–30 minutes**, against a §1.1 objective of 27 h–4 days of *continuous* decoding. Duty-cycling must be **block-granular**, not frame-granular: the receiver knows blockIndex from the header (§7.1), so it decodes block N at full attention and skips N+1 entirely. This doubles the number of passes but completes transfers where frame-granular duty cycling would never finish (frame-granular 50% duty on 25% erasure delivers only 0.60 K against the 1.03 K needed at dwell 1.6). No web API exposes SoC temperature, so sustained fps decline is the proxy (E17b). **Throttling discrimination:** Before applying duty-cycling, the receiver MUST distinguish sender-side throttling (E17a) from receiver-side throttling (E17b) using the multi-metric approach specified in `docs/notes/bf-3mnt-thermal-throttling-discrimination.md`. Sender-side throttling is detected when camera fps drops >30% while decode latency stays within +30%; in this case, the receiver MUST NOT duty-cycle. Receiver-side throttling is detected when decode latency increases >50% while camera fps stays within -20%; in this case, D27's block-granular duty-cycling applies. | `spike-results`, R11, `bf-3mnt` |\n248\t| **D25** | **Cap fountain degree at d ≤ 64** | Cuts encoder XOR **7.9×** at the adopted K = 768 (mean degree 106.3 → 13.5): 12.2 MB/s → 1.6 MB/s at 450 packets/s (R2 nominal: 2 packets/tile, 15 tiles, 15 fps). D6 forbids changing the distribution on faith, so it was **simulated**: at the adopted **K = 768** the cap costs **+1.6 points** (1.34% → 2.97% mean, p99 4.2%), and +1.9 pts at K = 1024. There is a cliff below it — cap 32 costs +4.9 pts with a bad p99, cap 16 costs **+55 pts**. 64 is the right side of the cliff with margin. | `sim/degree_cap_sim.py` |\n249\t| **D26** | **K is chosen by the SENDER at session start and MUST be conservative** | Decode cost lands on the receiver, whose CPU the sender cannot know (no back-channel). So the sender MUST assume the weaker device. K = 768 is the default floor; a sender-side setting MAY raise it when the user knows the receiver is a desktop, **but MUST NOT exceed K_MAX = 2048 to maintain I6a's 1 MB block-layer working set constraint**. Working set = K²/8 + K×L (matrix + block); at K = 2048 with L = 256 B this equals exactly 1 MB. The receiver derives K from the beacon and MUST refuse a stream whose K exceeds what it benchmarked locally. | §3.1, `src/core/params.ts` validateK() |\n250\t| **D20** | **Stream both ends; never materialise the file** | Multi-GB `ArrayBuffer` is not allocatable. `File.slice()` sender-side, OPFS receiver-side. | §3.2 |\n251\t| **D21** | **Per-packet header stays 13 bytes: file metadata lives in the beacon** | A 3-byte block index would have cost 23% more header. Moving `payloadLen`, filename, MIME, hash and block count into the periodic beacon pays for it exactly. Payload packets carry only what is needed to *place bytes*. | §7.1 |\n252\t| **D22** | **Resume is mandatory and first-class** | At 2.7–27 h for 1–10 GB, no transfer survives on user patience. Receiver persists the completed-block bitmap; incomplete blocks restart rather than persisting partial GE state. | §1.1, §8.3 |\n253\t| **D23** | **Estimate time before the user commits; refuse or warn at defined thresholds** | Thresholds are numeric (§13.1), not \"a threshold\". Estimate from *measured* rate once acquired. | §1.1 |\n254\t| **D24** | **Frames generated on demand and discarded; nothing pre-rendered** | The LT stream is endless — no finite frame set exists. One pass over 4 GB is ~550,000 frames = **4.2 TB** as `ImageData`. On-demand encode costs ~7% of one core. PRNG-derived indices make the sender **stateless**: frame *N* generates without replaying 1…*N*−1, which is what makes resume and repair nearly free. | §6.3.1 |\n255\t| D1 | **Tiled QR, not single QR** | 15 × v15 QR decode from one 1080p frame in 7.8 ms for ~7.5 KB user-visible payload (at 2 packets/tile: 15 tiles × 2 packets × 256 B = 7,680 B; 8.0 KB includes 13-byte headers). This vs 2,953 B for one v40 — ~2.5× for zero new decoder risk. | `beyond-qr` §10 |\n256\t| D2 | **QR v15 @ ECC L, ~15 tiles** | Bounded by the 4 **camera** px/module cliff (§2 — *not* screen px), not symbology density. EC L because the channel is erasure-dominated — redundancy belongs in the fountain code. L→H would cost 57% of payload for nothing. | `qr-encoding` |\n257\t| D3 | **zxing-wasm decoder, read `.bytes`** | Only credible multi-symbol decoder that returns real bytes — verified against 7 libraries with every byte value: exact in 100% of payloads. Bounded 9–26 ms where jsQR hit 1453 ms. Apache-2.0. | `browser-qr-scanning` |\n258\t| D4 | **node-qrcode encoder, mask pinned** | Pinning the mask is a 4.6–8× encode speedup — a bigger lever than library choice. Worker-safe. | `qr-encoding` |\n259\t| D5 | **LT fountain + harmonic distribution + GF(2) Gaussian elimination** | GE needs +1.2% overhead at K=1000 where peeling needs +180%. ~300 lines. **Re-measured at the adopted K = 768**: +1.34% mean / +2.5% p99 uncapped, +2.97% / +4.2% with D25's cap — inside §13.1's budget. See §18 R1 for the RaptorQ trigger. | `fountain-codes`, `sim/` |\n260\t| D6 | **Harmonic and GE are a coupled pair — never change one alone** | Harmonic + peeling is the worst cell measured and degrades as K grows. Fails only on large inputs, pointing away from the cause. Any change to the distribution (including D25's cap) MUST be simulated first. | `sim/` |\n261\t| D7 | **Index sets derived from a PRNG, never transmitted** | Seeded on `(streamId, blockIndex, seq)`. Zero index bytes on the wire. | `fountain-codes` |\n262\t| D8 | **Compress before blocking, to a staging file** | `CompressionStream` is native and streaming. Compress to OPFS first, then cut into fixed blocks — keeps K constant and derivable. Skip on already-compressed input (sample-detect). Staging MUST be wiped (§12, T4a). **Trade-off: with compression enabled, resume is NOT supported** (§8.3, `notes/bf-17s0-resume-compression-conflict.md`) — `CompressionStream` offers no determinism guarantee, so re-compression after staging is reaped (E11) would produce different blocks and silently corrupt the receiver's state. | `fountain-codes` |\n263\t| D9 | **Display at ≤ half the *measured* camera fps** | PixNet's rule. Faster produces only torn frames. | `beyond-qr` |\n264\t| D10 | **Every frame DC-balanced** | Stops auto-exposure hunting; throughput swings 2.4× on exposure. Also part of the photosensitivity mitigation (§20.1). | `custom-codec` |\n265\t| D11 | **A runtime calibration probe decides luma-vs-colour, not this document** | Two research threads reached opposite conclusions (§6.6). The probe measures the device. | `beyond-qr` §6.6 |\n266\t| D12 | **Dark-on-light, not dual-polarity** | Dual-polarity costs ~50% throughput. OLED ABL means mostly-white loses ~4× brightness — \"light\" means *moderate*. | `pwa-platform` |\n267\t| D13 | **Add to Home Screen is mandatory on iOS** | Safari deletes service-worker caches after 7 days; Home Screen apps are exempt. | `pwa-platform` |\n268\t| D14 | **`exposureCompensation: min`; measure delivered fps, never trust `getSettings()`** | A precondition for D9. Android delivers 15 fps while reporting 30/60; the fix measured 15.0 → 41.6 fps. Absent on iOS — hence \"measured\". | `browser-qr-scanning` §1.4 |\n269\t| D15 | **Fragment length `L` is fixed for the session — not per profile, not ever** | Change L and K changes, invalidating every packet already collected. | `link-adaptation-design` |\n270\t| D16 | **Sender mixes 2–4 robustness profiles *within every frame*; no negotiation in v1** | Packets are fungible, so the sender never has to choose. **Probing is free** — a probe tile that succeeds delivers real payload. Mixed within a frame so profiles cannot alias against camera fps. | `link-adaptation` |\n271\t| D17 | **Conservative beacon profile, re-emitted periodically** | WiFi's lowest basic rate. Enables late join and re-acquisition. Carries all file metadata (D21). | `link-adaptation-design` |\n272\t| D18a | **Phase 3: the ladder runs at FIXED weights. No control loop.** | OLLA is closed-loop and its error signal (`cameraPxPerModule`) is a **receiver-side** metric, but only the sender can change rungs and D16 says no negotiation in v1. A controller with no observable cannot run. The research places fixed-weight ladders at T2/Phase 3 and weight adaptation at T4/Phase 5; an earlier revision collapsed the two. **Fixed weights (frame-area fractions): R1 (conservative v10-L) = 15%, R2 (nominal v15-L) = 60%, R3 (aggressive v20-L) = 25%. Never drop any rung below 10% in steady state.** | `link-adaptation` §10.2 |\n273\t| D18b | **Phase 5: adapt ladder weights from LOCAL metrics only — OLLA structure, 1:9 up/down asymmetry, ~1 s window, 2 s dwell, immediate hard step-down** | Closed-loop density control oscillates; profile selection stays a **stateless lookup** so there is no state machine to get stuck in. \"Local\" means the sender's own signals (frame timing, accelerometer à la COBRA), never receiver feedback. | `link-adaptation` §10.3 |\n274\t| D18c | **Assume 20–30% residual erasure. This is an ASSUMPTION about the channel, not a controlled target.** | Nothing in v1 observes erasure (D18a), so calling it a \"target\" was wrong. 20–30% is the evidence base's figure; driving it lower would mean the ladder is too conservative and throughput is being left unused. Dwell is sized to survive the **top** of the band (§8.1), and the repair code (§8.2) covers the tail beyond it. | `link-adaptation` §9.3 |\n275\t\n276\t---\n277\t\n278\t## 5. Invariants\n279\t\n280\tViolating one of these is a correctness bug, not a tuning choice. Each has an\n281\tenforcement mechanism, because an invariant nothing checks is a comment.\n282\t\n283\t| # | Invariant | Enforced by |\n284\t|---|---|---|\n285\t| **I1** | Fragment length **L** MUST NOT change within a session (D15) | Session type makes `L` `readonly`; property test asserts a mid-session change throws |\n286\t| **I2** | The degree distribution and the decoder MUST change together (D6); any distribution change MUST be simulated before merge | `sim/` assertions ported into the test suite; CI gate G4 |\n287\t| **I3** | Fountain indices MUST be derived from `(streamId, blockIndex, seq)`, never transmitted (D7) | Golden test vector `(streamId, blockIndex, seq) → index set`, bit-exact across implementations |\n288\t| **I4** | The file MUST NOT be fully materialised in memory on either side (D20) | Phase 1 flat-memory test over a synthetic 4 GB stream |\n289\t| **I5** | **Exactly one payload block is GE-active at a time; the manifest stream has its own separate GE context** (bf-28b) | Session type permits two concurrent GE contexts: `active` for payload blocks and `manifestActive` for manifest blocks. Payload block-switch policy (`bf-2t1k`) governs when to switch: hold until rank K or N consecutive higher-index packets (default N=32). The manifest uses reserved `blockIndex = 0xFFFFFF` and `PacketFlags.Manifest`, providing clean separation from payload blocks. This is necessary because manifest blocks are interleaved with payload blocks (§7.6), and both require fountain decoding. |\n290\t| **I6a** | **Block-layer** working set MUST stay ≤ 1 MB regardless of file size (264 KB at the adopted design) | A5 headless block-layer memory assertion |\n291\t| **I6b** | **Whole-receiver** peak MUST stay ≤ 64 MB, and the decode pool MUST hold ≤ 4 in-flight `VideoFrame`s | Phase 3 instrumented run. A single 1080p RGBA frame is **7.9 MiB**, so this budget is dominated by the camera path, not the codec — which is why I6 had to be split |\n292\t| **I7** | Frames MUST be generated on demand, never pre-rendered (D24) | Ring buffer is bounded at 3; assertion on buffer depth |\n293\t| **I8** | A packet failing `fcrc` or `streamId` MUST be discarded, never applied | Unit test with corrupted and foreign packets |\n294\t| **I9** | A block MAY be written to OPFS before its hash arrives, but MUST NOT be surfaced to the user until verified | Test: blocks written before manifest arrives are not exported; verification failure prevents completion and triggers E-BLOCK-HASH |\n295\t| **I10** | Decoded output MUST be byte-identical to input | End-to-end property test, every phase |\n296\t\n297\t---\n298\t\n299\t## 6. Architecture\n300\t\n301\t### 6.1 Layering\n302\t\n303\t**Modulation is swappable**, and **the block layer bounds everything below it**.\n304\t\n305\t```\n306\t┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n307\t│ UI          role select · progress · file in/out · coach │\n308\t├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n309\t│ Session     metadata · compression · resume · verify     │\n310\t├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n311\t│ Block       file ⇄ 192 KB blocks · scheduling · bitmap   │\n312\t├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n313\t│ Fountain    LT encode (endless) / GF(2) GE decode        │\n314\t│             K = 768 · matrix 72.0 KB · CONSTANT          │\n315\t├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n316\t│ Framing     13-byte header + payload → packet bytes      │\n317\t├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n318\t│ Modulation  ◄──────────────────────── SWAPPABLE ────────►│\n319\t│   Stage 1   tiled monochrome QR                          │\n320\t│   Stage 2   + RGB channel tripling                       │\n321\t│   Stage 3   libcimbar-derived grid codec                 │\n322\t├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n323\t│ Transport   canvas render loop  /  camera capture loop   │\n324\t└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\n325\t```\n326\t\n327\t```ts\n328\tinterface Modulation {\n329\t  readonly packetsPerFrame: number;     // 1 plain, ~15 tiled, ~45 tripled\n330\t  readonly bytesPerPacket: number;      // = 13 + L\n331\t  encodeFrame(packets: Uint8Array[]): ImageData;\n332\t  decodeFrame(frame: VideoFrame): Uint8Array[];   // 0..n — never throws\n333\t}\n334\t```\n335\t\n336\t`decodeFrame` returning fewer packets than `packetsPerFrame` is the **normal case**.\n337\tNothing above this layer may care.\n338\t\n339\t### 6.2 Threads and ownership\n340\t\n341\tLayer boundaries and thread boundaries are **not** the same, which is worth stating\n342\texplicitly because it is a common source of bugs:\n343\t\n344\t| Component | Thread | Owns |\n345\t|---|---|---|\n346\t| UI, canvas paint | main | display |\n347\t| Frame encoder | worker | ring buffer (depth 3, I7) |\n348\t| QR decode pool | N workers | `VideoFrame` — MUST `close()` each or the pipeline stalls |\n349\t| GE decoder | 1 worker | the 72 KB matrix; single-owner, no sharing |\n350\t| OPFS writer | worker | `createSyncAccessHandle` is worker-only |\n351\t\n352\t**Backpressure policy:** if decode falls behind capture, camera frames are **dropped, not\n353\tqueued**. A queued frame is stale by the time it decodes, and queuing turns a throughput\n354\tproblem into a memory problem. Dropped frames are erasures, which the fountain code\n355\talready absorbs.\n356\t\n357\t### 6.3 Sender pipeline\n358\t\n359\t```\n360\tFile ──► [sample: compressible?] ──► CompressionStream ──► OPFS staging\n361\t  │            (D8, skip if not)                              │\n362\t  └──────────────── or straight through ─────────────────────┘\n363\t                                                              │\n364\t                                   cut into 192 KB blocks (D19)\n365\t                                                              │\n366\t                 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n367\t                 ▼                                            ▼\n368\t        beacon (D17/D21) every ~2 s          per block: slice → K=768 fragments\n369\t        filename · size · blockCount           → LT encode (d ≤ 64, D25)\n370\t        blockSize · L · K · hash · flags       → header → tile\n371\t                 │                                            │\n372\t                 └──────────────► frame mixer ◄───────────────┘\n373\t                                       │\n374\t                          ladder of 2–4 profiles (D16)\n375\t                                       │\n376\t                              DC-balance (D10) ──► canvas\n377\t                                       │\n378\t                     display at ≤ ½ measured camera fps (D9/D14)\n379\t```\n380\t\n381\tThe sender **dwells** on each block (§8.1), then advances, looping the file\n382\tcontinuously. It never terminates on its own — it cannot know when the receiver is done.\n383\t\n384\t> **Beacon clarification:** The beacon is a **packet** (distinguished by `PacketFlags.Beacon` in its header), not a separate frame. The \"frame mixer\" shown above combines beacon tiles (QR-encoded beacon packets) with payload tiles into the same displayed frames. This ensures minimal overhead: the sender emits beacon packets every ~2 seconds by replacing a few payload tiles in regular frames, rather than interrupting transmission with dedicated beacon frames.\n385\t\n386\t#### 6.3.1 Frames are generated on demand (D24)\n387\t\n388\tEvery arrow above is a **generator**, not an array.\n389\t\n390\t- **No finite frame set exists.** The LT encoder is rateless; how many frames a transfer\n391\t  needs depends on channel loss and is unknowable in advance.\n392\t- **One pass would not fit.** 4 GB ≈ 550,000 frames; as 1080p `ImageData` that is\n393\t  **4.2 TB**, ~55 GB even as PNGs.\n394\t- **On-demand is cheap.** ~0.29 ms per v15 tile (from 1.53 ms at v40, mask pinned) ×\n395\t  15 tiles × 15 fps ≈ **65 ms/sec, ~7% of one core**, plus ~2.3 ms/sec to render, plus\n396\t  **fountain XOR: 3.4 KB/packet at d ≤ 64 (D25) = 0.8 MB/s** at this geometry's\n397\t  **450 packets/s** (15 tiles × 2 packets/tile × 15 fps, using the R2 nominal rung) —\n398\t  negligible, but only because of the cap. Uncapped it is 6.1 MB/s\n399\t  at K = 768, and was 91.8 MB/s at the old K = 16,384.\n400\t\n401\tBecause indices derive from a PRNG (D7), the sender is **stateless**: frame *N* generates\n402\tdirectly without replaying 1…*N*−1. That is what makes resume and repair nearly free.\n403\t\n404\t**Implementation:** worker generator → ring buffer (depth 3) → main thread paints via\n405\t`rAF`. Deeper buffering is wasted memory (I7).\n406\t\n407\t#### 6.3.2 Shape the code region to the CAMERA, not the screen\n408\t\n409\tMeasured, and worth ~4–5× on its own. The receiver's camera has a fixed aspect and a fixed\n410\tpixel count; the sender's screen has a different one. What matters is **camera px per module**\n411\t(§2), and that is set by how much of the capture the code region fills.\n412\t\n413\tA 1920×1080 landscape code region imaged by a portrait 1080×1920 capture yields **M = 0.5625** —\n414\tso 4 screen px/module is only 2.25 camera px/module, below the cliff. Rendering the *same*\n415\tpayload into a **portrait-shaped region** inverts this:\n416\t\n417\t| Code region on screen | M | Camera px/module @ 2 screen px | Tiles | QR cap/frame | Payload/frame |\n418\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n419\t| 1920×1080 (naive: fill the screen) | 0.56 | 1.13 — **far below cliff** | 15 | 8.8 KB | 7.5 KB |\n420\t| 1080×1080 square | 1.00 | 2.00 — below cliff | 9 | 5.3 KB | 4.5 KB |\n421\t| **540×960 portrait** | **2.00** | **4.00 — above cliff** | 15 | **8.8 KB** | **7.5 KB** |\n422\t\n423\tSame tile count and same bytes per frame as the naive layout, but *above* the cliff instead of\n424\tbelow it — so yield goes from roughly a fifth to near-total. **The sender MUST size the code\n425\tregion to the receiver's capture aspect, not to its own display.** Since there is no\n426\tback-channel, it cannot know that aspect: expose it as a user-visible setting (portrait /\n427\tlandscape receiver) **defaulting to portrait, which is how phones are held — and portrait is\n428\ta fully supported mode, not a degraded one.** The 540×960 portrait region above clears the\n429\tcliff (4.00 camera px/module) at the *same* 7.5 KB/frame payload as the naive landscape\n430\tlayout. **Phase 3's ≥ 20 KB/s gate MUST pass with the receiver held portrait, unaided** —\n431\tthat is the default, unassisted case, not a stretch goal.\n432\t\n433\t**Packets-per-tile basis.** The R2 nominal rung (v16-L, 60% of tiles in steady state per D18a)\n434\tcarries **2 packets per tile**. Each packet is 269 B (13-byte header + 256 B payload), so\n435\t2 packets = 538 B per tile, which fits within v16-L's 586 B capacity. The **user-visible payload**\n436\tis 15 tiles × 2 packets/tile × 256 B = **7,680 B/frame ≈ 7.5 KB/frame**, matching the table\n437\tabove (per §13.2, all throughput figures quote user-visible bytes, not wire bytes). The **8.8 KB/frame\n438\tQR capacity** is 15 tiles × 586 B (v16-L capacity). At 15 fps, this geometry delivers\n439\t**7.5 KB × 15 fps = 112.5 KB/s payload rate** (or ~113 KB/s) before fountain overhead\n440\tand erasure loss.\n441\t\n442\t**Two routes to the same M; landscape is a free bonus, not a requirement.** Physically holding\n443\tthe receiver in landscape puts the screen's long axis on the camera's long axis — **1.78×,\n444\tfree, and it does not require halving screen px/module the way the portrait-region layout\n445\tdoes** — so it is worth *offering* to a user willing to turn the phone. But the app MUST NOT\n446\tdepend on the user doing so: the sender-side portrait region (above) is the primary,\n447\talways-on path, and landscape is strictly an optional upgrade for extra margin on top of it.\n448\t\n449\tVerified negative: forcing the receiver's *OS* orientation does not help — sensor mapping\n450\tfollows the device body, not the UI. Since portrait is the supported default, this mostly\n451\tdoesn't matter; it only matters for the optional landscape upgrade, which needs a *physical*\n452\tturn (§11 `E-ORIENTATION`, reframed below as a tip, not a requirement).\n453\t\n454\t### 6.4 Receiver pipeline\n455\t\n456\t```\n457\tgetUserMedia ──► exposureCompensation:min (D14) ──► measure real fps (rVFC, ~1 s)\n458\t      │\n459\t      └──► requestVideoFrameCallback ──► MediaStreamTrackProcessor*\n460\t                                                │\n461\t                              ROI crop (conditional — see §6.4)\n462\t                                                │\n463\t                              ┌─────────────────┴──── Worker pool ────┐\n464\t                              ▼                                       ▼\n465\t                      zxing readBarcodes                     [Stage 2: split\n466\t                      (all symbols, .bytes)                   R/G/B, stretch, ×3]\n467\t                              │\n468\t                    header parse ──► fcrc ──► streamId lock ──► route by blockIndex\n469\t                              │                                        │\n470\t                     beacon? This is *not* the whole-receiver figure; see I6a/I6b in §5.\n486\t\n487\tThree rules that are cheap to implement and expensive to omit:\n488\t\n489\t- **Measure fps, never trust it.** `getSettings()` reports 30/60 while the camera\n490\t  delivers 15.\n491\t- **Crop to ROI before decoding — but the 9× is conditional.** Measured 8.6× (56.9 → 6.6 ms)\n492\t  *when the code occupies part of the frame*. Everything else is explanation.\n\n---\n\n## 1. Objective\n\n> **A static website that accepts a file from the user and turns it into a visual\n> transmission on screen, which a second device running the same page receives through\n> its camera and reconstructs into the original file.**\n>\n> **It must handle large files — on the order of multiple gigabytes.**\n\n- **Static.** No backend. Files on a CDN, works offline, auditable once and trusted\n  thereafter. There is nowhere to upload anything *to*.\n- **Same page, both roles.** One deployment; the user picks sender or receiver.\n- **Screen → camera is the only channel.** Strictly one-way, lossy, low-bandwidth.\n- **Multi-gigabyte.** The requirement that most shapes the architecture (§3).\n\n### 1.1 The honest framing of \"multiple gigabytes\"\n\nMulti-GB support is an **architectural** requirement, not a performance promise. The\ndesign must never *forbid* a large file, run out of memory, or blow up super-linearly.\nBut the channel's physics are what they are:\n\n| File size | Stage 1 (30 KB/s) | Stage 2 (60 KB/s) | Stage 3 (106 KB/s) |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 100 MB | 57 min | 28 min | 16 min |\n| **1 GB** | **9.7 h** | **4.9 h** | **2.7 h** |\n| **10 GB** | **4.0 days** | **2.0 days** | **27.5 h** |\n| 100 GB | 40.5 days | 20.2 days | 11.4 days |\n| 1 TB | 414 days | 207 days | 117 days |\n\n> All figures are **user-visible file bytes**, not wire bytes. See §13.2 — with\n> compression on, the two differ by 3–10× on compressible input, and quoting the wrong\n> one would overstate throughput.\n\n**Gigabytes are hours-to-days. Terabytes are months.** Three design consequences follow,\nand they are as load-bearing as any coding decision:\n\n1. **Resume is not optional** (D22). Nobody holds a phone for 27 hours.\n2. **Neither side may hold the file in memory** (D20).\n3. **The app states the estimated time before the user commits** (D23). Letting someone\n   start a 40-day transfer without saying so is a product failure, not an edge case.\n\n---\n\n## 2. Glossary\n\nSeveral of these words are overloaded in the surrounding literature, and two of them\n(*block*, *frame*) mean different things in different research documents. Within this\nplan they mean exactly this:\n\n| Term | Meaning here |\n|---|---|\n| **Fragment** | The atomic unit the fountain code operates over. Fixed length **L** for the whole session (D15). |\n| **K** | Number of fragments in one block. Derived as `blockSize / L`; never transmitted (D7). |\n| **Block** | A contiguous slice of the (possibly compressed) payload, cut into K fragments and fountain-coded independently. **Always means this** — never \"fountain block\" or \"QR block\". |\n| **Packet** | One fountain-coded symbol: 13-byte header + L payload bytes. The unit a tile carries. |\n| **Tile** | One QR symbol on screen. Carries exactly one packet. |\n| **Frame** | One displayed image, containing a grid of tiles. **Never** a video frame — those are *camera frames*. |\n| **Camera frame** | One image captured by the receiver's camera. |\n| **Beacon** | A special **packet** carrying file-level metadata instead of payload. Beacon packets are encoded into tiles and mixed into display frames by the frame mixer (D17, §7.2). |\n| **Profile** | A modulation configuration: QR version, module pixel size, tile count. Several coexist per frame (D16). |\n| **Dwell** | How many packets the sender emits for one block before advancing (§8.1). |\n| **Screen px** | A pixel on the *sender's display*. What the renderer controls. |\n| **Camera px** | A pixel in the *receiver's captured frame*. What the decoder actually sees. |\n| **px/module** | **Always CAMERA px per module unless explicitly written \"screen px/module\".** The 4 px/module decode cliff is a *camera*-pixel figure. Conflating the two put every S2/S3 optical run below the cliff — see `../notes/spike-results.md` §S3. |\n| **Magnification** | `camera_px_per_module = screen_px_per_module × M`, where `M` = (capture width across the code region) / (code region width in screen px). A 1920-px-wide landscape code region filling a 1080-px-wide portrait capture gives **M = 0.5625**, so 4 screen px/module is only **2.25 camera px/module**. |\n| **Erasure** | A packet that did not arrive or failed validation. Never a corrupted packet — those are discarded, not used. |\n| **Stage** | A modulation generation: 1 = tiled mono QR, 2 = + RGB tripling, 3 = custom grid codec. |\n| **Pass** | One complete traversal of every block by the sender. |\n\n---\n\n## 3. What multi-gigabyte breaks, and the fix\n\nFour assumptions in the pre-multi-GB design do not survive contact with a 4 GB file.\n\n### 3.1 The fountain decoder does not scale — in TIME, not memory\n\nThis is the correction the plan review surfaced, and it matters because the first\nversion of this section got it half right.\n\nD5 chose an LT code with a **Gaussian elimination** decoder, verified at\n[`sim/`](../research/sim/). GE costs O(K²) in *memory* and O(K³) in *bit operations*.\nThe original block-layer decision sized K from the memory term alone and concluded 4 MB\nblocks (K = 16,384) were fine because the coefficient matrix is only 32 MB.\n\n**The memory term was never the binding constraint. Time is.**\n\nEach arriving packet is reduced against up to `rank` stored pivot rows; each row\noperation XORs the coefficient mask (K/8 bytes) *and* the payload (L bytes). Reaching\nfull rank costs `W = 2 · (K²/2) · (K/8 + L) = K² · (K/8 + L)` bytes of memory traffic,\nand the block only lasts `K·L / R` seconds at wire rate R — so the decoder must\n**sustain**:\n\n```\nrequired = W / (K·L/R) = K · (K/8 + L) · R / L    bytes/sec\n```\n\n> The leading factor is **1, not 2** — the 2 and the /2 in `W` cancel. A previous\n> revision of this section printed `2 · K · (K/8 + L) · R / L` and was 2× too\n> pessimistic in every derived figure. Gate **G7** now diffs this section against the\n> model so the class of error cannot recur.\n\nAll figures below are emitted by\n[`sim/ge_cost_model.py`](../research/sim/ge_cost_model.py) — this section quotes the\nmodel rather than reasoning beside it. **All rows at Stage 1 (R = 30 KB/s)**, so they\nare comparable:\n\n| K | L | Block | Matrix | Work/block | Sustained need | |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 1,000 | 1260 | 1.2 MB | 122.1 KB | 1.3 GB | 33.8 MB/s | research baseline |\n| 1,500 | 1260 | 1.8 MB | 274.7 KB | 3.0 GB | 52.9 MB/s | research partitioning ceiling |\n| 4,000 | 1260 | 4.8 MB | 1.9 MB | 26.2 GB | 171.6 MB/s | research called this **\"too slow\"** |\n| **16,384** | **256** | **4.0 MB** | **32.0 MB** | **576.0 GB** | **4.5 GB/s** | **23× over budget** |\n\nThe plan's own evidence base\n([`fountain-codes-and-protocol.md`](../research/fountain-codes-and-protocol.md) §2.6)\nstates: *\"Cost scales as K², so it must be bounded. At K = 4000 the decode work is ~16×\nthat of K = 1000 (~6 GB of XOR) — too slow\"* and recommends *\"source-block partitioning\nabove K ≈ 1500\"*. **K = 16,384 was 11× past that ceiling.**\n\nIt was worse than a simple overshoot: shrinking L to 256 B to fit small tiles made the\nmask term (K/8 = 2048 B) dominate the payload term (256 B) by 8×, so the decode problem\ngot *harder* as a side effect of a decision made for a different reason.\n\n**Two further findings from the model:**\n\n- **A faster wire rate makes decode harder** — same work, less time to do it. So K MUST\n  be sized for the *fastest* stage we intend to reach (Stage 3, 106 KB/s), not the\n  slowest. This is counterintuitive and is why the original error was easy to make.\n- **The sender's cost was unbudgeted too.** §6.3.1 counted QR encode and render but not\n  the fountain XOR. At uncapped harmonic degree and K = 16,384 that is 398 KB of XOR\n  per packet — **91.8 MB/s** at the old 225 packets/s (1 packet/tile), or **183.6 MB/s**\n  at the adopted 450 packets/s (2 packets/tile at R2 nominal), on top of everything\n  else. Hence D25.\n\n**Fix — D19:** K = **768**, L = **256 B**, block = **192.0 KB**.\n\n| | Was | Now |\n|---|---|---|\n| K | 16,384 | **768** |\n| L | 256 B | **256 B** (unchanged — see §3.1.1) |\n| Block | 4 MB | **192.0 KB** |\n| GE matrix | 32.0 MB | **72.0 KB** |\n| Block-layer working set | ~36 MB (claimed) | **264.0 KB** |\n| Sustained need @ Stage 3 | 14.9 GB/s | **114.6 MB/s** |\n\n*Both \"sustained need\" figures are at Stage 3, so they compare like with like. The\n4.5 GB/s in the table above is the same design at Stage 1.*\n\n**K_max at Stage 3 is 1152.** We adopt **768** deliberately below the ceiling —\nD26 requires the sender to assume the weaker receiver, and the 200 MB/s budget is\nitself an unmeasured estimate (§18 R1). Margin at Stage 3: **1.74×**.\n\n| K | Block | Stage 1 | Stage 2 | Stage 3 | |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 512 | 128.0 KB | 19.7 MB/s | 39.3 MB/s | 69.5 MB/s | 2.88× margin |\n| **768** | **192.0 KB** | **32.4 MB/s** | **64.9 MB/s** | **114.6 MB/s** | **adopted, 1.74× margin** |\n| 1024 | 256.0 KB | 47.2 MB/s | 94.4 MB/s | 166.7 MB/s | 1.20× margin |\n| 1152 | 288.0 KB | 55.3 MB/s | 110.6 MB/s | 195.4 MB/s | 1.02× — the ceiling |\n| 1536 | 384.0 KB | 82.6 MB/s | 165.2 MB/s | 291.8 MB/s | 1.5× **over** at Stage 3 |\n\n### 3.1.1 L is set by the *conservative* ladder rung, not the nominal one\n\nA revision of this plan briefly set L = 507 B (\"one packet per v15 tile\") and broke\nD16's ladder. D15's source note states the governing rule plainly: **pick L to fit the\nsmallest tile any profile would use.** At L = 507 the packet is 520 B and the\nconservative rung, v10-L, holds **271 B** — so it could carry **zero** packets, only\nbeacons. That destroys the ladder's one load-bearing property: *a mis-guessed profile\nyields zero; a ladder always yields something.*\n\n**Rungs are therefore defined by packet count, with the QR version chosen to fit** —\nnot the reverse. At L = 256 B, packet = 13 + 256 = **269 B**:\n\n| Rung | Packets | Needs | QR version | Capacity | Waste |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| R1 conservative | 1 | 269 B | v10-L | 271 B | 2 B |\n| R2 nominal | 2 | 538 B | v16-L | 586 B | 48 B |\n| R3 aggressive | 3 | 807 B | v20-L | 858 B | 51 B |\n| R4 (probe only) | 4 | 1076 B | v23-L | 1091 B | 15 B |\n\nWaste stays ≤ 51 B on every rung. The pressure that motivated raising L has also\ngone: at K = 768 the mask term is K/8 = 96 B against a 256 B payload (27%), not the\n8× dominance that made L = 256 pathological at K = 16,384.\n\n**A rung MUST carry a whole number of packets.** Partial packets across tiles would\ncouple tiles together and destroy the independence D1 depends on.\n\n### 3.2 Neither side can hold the file in memory\n\nA multi-GB `Uint8Array` is not allocatable (Chrome's `ArrayBuffer` ceiling is ~2 GB;\nSafari's is lower), and would get a phone tab killed regardless.\n\n**Fix — D20:** stream both ends. `File.slice()` on the sender, OPFS on the receiver, one\nblock resident at a time.\n\n### 3.3 The whole-file hash cannot be computed in one pass\n\n`crypto.subtle.digest` has **no streaming API** — it takes one buffer.\n\n**Fix:** per-block hashes (cheap, and they let each block be written as it completes,\nthen verified retroactively once the manifest arrives) plus an optional whole-file hash\nfrom an incremental WASM hasher. See §7.4 for how this interacts with `streamId`.\n\n### 3.4 Miss recovery gets expensive as blocks multiply\n\nAt 192 KB per block a 4 GB file is ~21,800 blocks. Sequential dwell means a block missed\non pass 1 waits for pass 2 — hours. **Fix:** the repair code (§8.2), which makes recovery\nsub-minute and is why smaller blocks are affordable.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Decisions\n\n| # | Decision | Rationale | Source |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| **D19** | **Block layer: independent 192.0 KB blocks, K = 768, L = 256 B** | GE cost is bound by *time*, not memory (§3.1). K = 768 keeps pace at Stage 3's 106 KB/s (114.6 MB/s needed, **1.74x margin**) within a conservative 200 MB/s phone-JS budget; matrix is 72.0 KB and the block-layer working set 264.0 KB, flat regardless of file size. K_max is 1152; 768 is deliberate conservatism per D26. **L is set by the conservative ladder rung** (S3.1.1), not the nominal one. What RFC 6330 calls source blocks. | §3.1, `sim/ge_cost_model.py` |\n| **D27** | **The receiver duty-cycles BLOCKS under receiver-side thermal pressure; multi-GB is framed as multi-session** | Measured: a Pixel 6 hit 70 °C and its throttling threshold in **20–30 minutes**, against a §1.1 objective of 27 h–4 days of *continuous* decoding. Duty-cycling must be **block-granular**, not frame-granular: the receiver knows blockIndex from the header (§7.1), so it decodes block N at full attention and skips N+1 entirely. This doubles the number of passes but completes transfers where frame-granular duty cycling would never finish (frame-granular 50% duty on 25% erasure delivers only 0.60 K against the 1.03 K needed at dwell 1.6). No web API exposes SoC temperature, so sustained fps decline is the proxy (E17b). **Throttling discrimination:** Before applying duty-cycling, the receiver MUST distinguish sender-side throttling (E17a) from receiver-side throttling (E17b) using the multi-metric approach specified in `docs/notes/bf-3mnt-thermal-throttling-discrimination.md`. Sender-side throttling is detected when camera fps drops >30% while decode latency stays within +30%; in this case, the receiver MUST NOT duty-cycle. Receiver-side throttling is detected when decode latency increases >50% while camera fps stays within -20%; in this case, D27's block-granular duty-cycling applies. | `spike-results`, R11, `bf-3mnt` |\n| **D25** | **Cap fountain degree at d ≤ 64** | Cuts encoder XOR **7.9×** at the adopted K = 768 (mean degree 106.3 → 13.5): 12.2 MB/s → 1.6 MB/s at 450 packets/s (R2 nominal: 2 packets/tile, 15 tiles, 15 fps). D6 forbids changing the distribution on faith, so it was **simulated**: at the adopted **K = 768** the cap costs **+1.6 points** (1.34% → 2.97% mean, p99 4.2%), and +1.9 pts at K = 1024. There is a cliff below it — cap 32 costs +4.9 pts with a bad p99, cap 16 costs **+55 pts**. 64 is the right side of the cliff with margin. | `sim/degree_cap_sim.py` |\n| **D26** | **K is chosen by the SENDER at session start and MUST be conservative** | Decode cost lands on the receiver, whose CPU the sender cannot know (no back-channel). So the sender MUST assume the weaker device. K = 768 is the default floor; a sender-side setting MAY raise it when the user knows the receiver is a desktop, **but MUST NOT exceed K_MAX = 2048 to maintain I6a's 1 MB block-layer working set constraint**. Working set = K²/8 + K×L (matrix + block); at K = 2048 with L = 256 B this equals exactly 1 MB. The receiver derives K from the beacon and MUST refuse a stream whose K exceeds what it benchmarked locally. | §3.1, `src/core/params.ts` validateK() |\n| **D20** | **Stream both ends; never materialise the file** | Multi-GB `ArrayBuffer` is not allocatable. `File.slice()` sender-side, OPFS receiver-side. | §3.2 |\n| **D21** | **Per-packet header stays 13 bytes: file metadata lives in the beacon** | A 3-byte block index would have cost 23% more header. Moving `payloadLen`, filename, MIME, hash and block count into the periodic beacon pays for it exactly. Payload packets carry only what is needed to *place bytes*. | §7.1 |\n| **D22** | **Resume is mandatory and first-class** | At 2.7–27 h for 1–10 GB, no transfer survives on user patience. Receiver persists the completed-block bitmap; incomplete blocks restart rather than persisting partial GE state. | §1.1, §8.3 |\n| **D23** | **Estimate time before the user commits; refuse or warn at defined thresholds** | Thresholds are numeric (§13.1), not \"a threshold\". Estimate from *measured* rate once acquired. | §1.1 |\n| **D24** | **Frames generated on demand and discarded; nothing pre-rendered** | The LT stream is endless — no finite frame set exists. One pass over 4 GB is ~550,000 frames = **4.2 TB** as `ImageData`. On-demand encode costs ~7% of one core. PRNG-derived indices make the sender **stateless**: frame *N* generates without replaying 1…*N*−1, which is what makes resume and repair nearly free. | §6.3.1 |\n| D1 | **Tiled QR, not single QR** | 15 × v15 QR decode from one 1080p frame in 7.8 ms for ~7.5 KB user-visible payload (at 2 packets/tile: 15 tiles × 2 packets × 256 B = 7,680 B; 8.0 KB includes 13-byte headers). This vs 2,953 B for one v40 — ~2.5× for zero new decoder risk. | `beyond-qr` §10 |\n| D2 | **QR v15 @ ECC L, ~15 tiles** | Bounded by the 4 **camera** px/module cliff (§2 — *not* screen px), not symbology density. EC L because the channel is erasure-dominated — redundancy belongs in the fountain code. L→H would cost 57% of payload for nothing. | `qr-encoding` |\n| D3 | **zxing-wasm decoder, read `.bytes`** | Only credible multi-symbol decoder that returns real bytes — verified against 7 libraries with every byte value: exact in 100% of payloads. Bounded 9–26 ms where jsQR hit 1453 ms. Apache-2.0. | `browser-qr-scanning` |\n| D4 | **node-qrcode encoder, mask pinned** | Pinning the mask is a 4.6–8× encode speedup — a bigger lever than library choice. Worker-safe. | `qr-encoding` |\n| D5 | **LT fountain + harmonic distribution + GF(2) Gaussian elimination** | GE needs +1.2% overhead at K=1000 where peeling needs +180%. ~300 lines. **Re-measured at the adopted K = 768**: +1.34% mean / +2.5% p99 uncapped, +2.97% / +4.2% with D25's cap — inside §13.1's budget. See §18 R1 for the RaptorQ trigger. | `fountain-codes`, `sim/` |\n| D6 | **Harmonic and GE are a coupled pair — never change one alone** | Harmonic + peeling is the worst cell measured and degrades as K grows. Fails only on large inputs, pointing away from the cause. Any change to the distribution (including D25's cap) MUST be simulated first. | `sim/` |\n| D7 | **Index sets derived from a PRNG, never transmitted** | Seeded on `(streamId, blockIndex, seq)`. Zero index bytes on the wire. | `fountain-codes` |\n| D8 | **Compress before blocking, to a staging file** | `CompressionStream` is native and streaming. Compress to OPFS first, then cut into fixed blocks — keeps K constant and derivable. Skip on already-compressed input (sample-detect). Staging MUST be wiped (§12, T4a). **Trade-off: with compression enabled, resume is NOT supported** (§8.3, `notes/bf-17s0-resume-compression-conflict.md`) — `CompressionStream` offers no determinism guarantee, so re-compression after staging is reaped (E11) would produce different blocks and silently corrupt the receiver's state. | `fountain-codes` |\n| D9 | **Display at ≤ half the *measured* camera fps** | PixNet's rule. Faster produces only torn frames. | `beyond-qr` |\n| D10 | **Every frame DC-balanced** | Stops auto-exposure hunting; throughput swings 2.4× on exposure. Also part of the photosensitivity mitigation (§20.1). | `custom-codec` |\n| D11 | **A runtime calibration probe decides luma-vs-colour, not this document** | Two research threads reached opposite conclusions (§6.6). The probe measures the device. | `beyond-qr` §6.6 |\n| D12 | **Dark-on-light, not dual-polarity** | Dual-polarity costs ~50% throughput. OLED ABL means mostly-white loses ~4× brightness — \"light\" means *moderate*. | `pwa-platform` |\n| D13 | **Add to Home Screen is mandatory on iOS** | Safari deletes service-worker caches after 7 days; Home Screen apps are exempt. | `pwa-platform` |\n| D14 | **`exposureCompensation: min`; measure delivered fps, never trust `getSettings()`** | A precondition for D9. Android delivers 15 fps while reporting 30/60; the fix measured 15.0 → 41.6 fps. Absent on iOS — hence \"measured\". | `browser-qr-scanning` §1.4 |\n| D15 | **Fragment length `L` is fixed for the session — not per profile, not ever** | Change L and K changes, invalidating every packet already collected. | `link-adaptation-design` |\n| D16 | **Sender mixes 2–4 robustness profiles *within every frame*; no negotiation in v1** | Packets are fungible, so the sender never has to choose. **Probing is free** — a probe tile that succeeds delivers real payload. Mixed within a frame so profiles cannot alias against camera fps. | `link-adaptation` |\n| D17 | **Conservative beacon profile, re-emitted periodically** | WiFi's lowest basic rate. Enables late join and re-acquisition. Carries all file metadata (D21). | `link-adaptation-design` |\n| D18a | **Phase 3: the ladder runs at FIXED weights. No control loop.** | OLLA is closed-loop and its error signal (`cameraPxPerModule`) is a **receiver-side** metric, but only the sender can change rungs and D16 says no negotiation in v1. A controller with no observable cannot run. The research places fixed-weight ladders at T2/Phase 3 and weight adaptation at T4/Phase 5; an earlier revision collapsed the two. **Fixed weights (frame-area fractions): R1 (conservative v10-L) = 15%, R2 (nominal v15-L) = 60%, R3 (aggressive v20-L) = 25%. Never drop any rung below 10% in steady state.** | `link-adaptation` §10.2 |\n| D18b | **Phase 5: adapt ladder weights from LOCAL metrics only — OLLA structure, 1:9 up/down asymmetry, ~1 s window, 2 s dwell, immediate hard step-down** | Closed-loop density control oscillates; profile selection stays a **stateless lookup** so there is no state machine to get stuck in. \"Local\" means the sender's own signals (frame timing, accelerometer à la COBRA), never receiver feedback. | `link-adaptation` §10.3 |\n| D18c | **Assume 20–30% residual erasure. This is an ASSUMPTION about the channel, not a controlled target.** | Nothing in v1 observes erasure (D18a), so calling it a \"target\" was wrong. 20–30% is the evidence base's figure; driving it lower would mean the ladder is too conservative and throughput is being left unused. Dwell is sized to survive the **top** of the band (§8.1), and the repair code (§8.2) covers the tail beyond it. | `link-adaptation` §9.3 |\n\n---\n\n## 5. Invariants\n\nViolating one of these is a correctness bug, not a tuning choice. Each has an\nenforcement mechanism, because an invariant nothing checks is a comment.\n\n| # | Invariant | Enforced by |\n|---|---|---|\n| **I1** | Fragment length **L** MUST NOT change within a session (D15) | Session type makes `L` `readonly`; property test asserts a mid-session change throws |\n| **I2** | The degree distribution and the decoder MUST change together (D6); any distribution change MUST be simulated before merge | `sim/` assertions ported into the test suite; CI gate G4 |\n| **I3** | Fountain indices MUST be derived from `(streamId, blockIndex, seq)`, never transmitted (D7) | Golden test vector `(streamId, blockIndex, seq) → index set`, bit-exact across implementations |\n| **I4** | The file MUST NOT be fully materialised in memory on either side (D20) | Phase 1 flat-memory test over a synthetic 4 GB stream |\n| **I5** | **Exactly one payload block is GE-active at a time; the manifest stream has its own separate GE context** (bf-28b) | Session type permits two concurrent GE contexts: `active` for payload blocks and `manifestActive` for manifest blocks. Payload block-switch policy (`bf-2t1k`) governs when to switch: hold until rank K or N consecutive higher-index packets (default N=32). The manifest uses reserved `blockIndex = 0xFFFFFF` and `PacketFlags.Manifest`, providing clean separation from payload blocks. This is necessary because manifest blocks are interleaved with payload blocks (§7.6), and both require fountain decoding. |\n| **I6a** | **Block-layer** working set MUST stay ≤ 1 MB regardless of file size (264 KB at the adopted design) | A5 headless block-layer memory assertion |\n| **I6b** | **Whole-receiver** peak MUST stay ≤ 64 MB, and the decode pool MUST hold ≤ 4 in-flight `VideoFrame`s | Phase 3 instrumented run. A single 1080p RGBA frame is **7.9 MiB**, so this budget is dominated by the camera path, not the codec — which is why I6 had to be split |\n| **I7** | Frames MUST be generated on demand, never pre-rendered (D24) | Ring buffer is bounded at 3; assertion on buffer depth |\n| **I8** | A packet failing `fcrc` or `streamId` MUST be discarded, never applied | Unit test with corrupted and foreign packets |\n| **I9** | A block MAY be written to OPFS before its hash arrives, but MUST NOT be surfaced to the user until verified | Test: blocks written before manifest arrives are not exported; verification failure prevents completion and triggers E-BLOCK-HASH |\n| **I10** | Decoded output MUST be byte-identical to input | End-to-end property test, every phase |\n\n---\n\n## 6. Architecture\n\n### 6.1 Layering\n\n**Modulation is swappable**, and **the block layer bounds everything below it**.\n\n```\n┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐\n│ UI          role select · progress · file in/out · coach │\n├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n│ Session     metadata · compression · resume · verify     │\n├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n│ Block       file ⇄ 192 KB blocks · scheduling · bitmap   │\n├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n│ Fountain    LT encode (endless) / GF(2) GE decode        │\n│             K = 768 · matrix 72.0 KB · CONSTANT          │\n├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n│ Framing     13-byte header + payload → packet bytes      │\n├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n│ Modulation  ◄──────────────────────── SWAPPABLE ────────►│\n│   Stage 1   tiled monochrome QR                          │\n│   Stage 2   + RGB channel tripling                       │\n│   Stage 3   libcimbar-derived grid codec                 │\n├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n│ Transport   canvas render loop  /  camera capture loop   │\n└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\n```ts\ninterface Modulation {\n  readonly packetsPerFrame: number;     // 1 plain, ~15 tiled, ~45 tripled\n  readonly bytesPerPacket: number;      // = 13 + L\n  encodeFrame(packets: Uint8Array[]): ImageData;\n  decodeFrame(frame: VideoFrame): Uint8Array[];   // 0..n — never throws\n}\n```\n\n`decodeFrame` returning fewer packets than `packetsPerFrame` is the **normal case**.\nNothing above this layer may care.\n\n### 6.2 Threads and ownership\n\nLayer boundaries and thread boundaries are **not** the same, which is worth stating\nexplicitly because it is a common source of bugs:\n\n| Component | Thread | Owns |\n|---|---|---|\n| UI, canvas paint | main | display |\n| Frame encoder | worker | ring buffer (depth 3, I7) |\n| QR decode pool | N workers | `VideoFrame` — MUST `close()` each or the pipeline stalls |\n| GE decoder | 1 worker | the 72 KB matrix; single-owner, no sharing |\n| OPFS writer | worker | `createSyncAccessHandle` is worker-only |\n\n**Backpressure policy:** if decode falls behind capture, camera frames are **dropped, not\nqueued**. A queued frame is stale by the time it decodes, and queuing turns a throughput\nproblem into a memory problem. Dropped frames are erasures, which the fountain code\nalready absorbs.\n\n### 6.3 Sender pipeline\n\n```\nFile ──► [sample: compressible?] ──► CompressionStream ──► OPFS staging\n  │            (D8, skip if not)                              │\n  └──────────────── or straight through ─────────────────────┘\n                                                              │\n                                   cut into 192 KB blocks (D19)\n                                                              │\n                 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┤\n                 ▼                                            ▼\n        beacon (D17/D21) every ~2 s          per block: slice → K=768 fragments\n        filename · size · blockCount           → LT encode (d ≤ 64, D25)\n        blockSize · L · K · hash · flags       → header → tile\n                 │                                            │\n                 └──────────────► frame mixer ◄───────────────┘\n                                       │\n                          ladder of 2–4 profiles (D16)\n                                       │\n                              DC-balance (D10) ──► canvas\n                                       │\n                     display at ≤ ½ measured camera fps (D9/D14)\n```\n\nThe sender **dwells** on each block (§8.1), then advances, looping the file\ncontinuously. It never terminates on its own — it cannot know when the receiver is done.\n\n> **Beacon clarification:** The beacon is a **packet** (distinguished by `PacketFlags.Beacon` in its header), not a separate frame. The \"frame mixer\" shown above combines beacon tiles (QR-encoded beacon packets) with payload tiles into the same displayed frames. This ensures minimal overhead: the sender emits beacon packets every ~2 seconds by replacing a few payload tiles in regular frames, rather than interrupting transmission with dedicated beacon frames.\n\n#### 6.3.1 Frames are generated on demand (D24)\n\nEvery arrow above is a **generator**, not an array.\n\n- **No finite frame set exists.** The LT encoder is rateless; how many frames a transfer\n  needs depends on channel loss and is unknowable in advance.\n- **One pass would not fit.** 4 GB ≈ 550,000 frames; as 1080p `ImageData` that is\n  **4.2 TB**, ~55 GB even as PNGs.\n- **On-demand is cheap.** ~0.29 ms per v15 tile (from 1.53 ms at v40, mask pinned) ×\n  15 tiles × 15 fps ≈ **65 ms/sec, ~7% of one core**, plus ~2.3 ms/sec to render, plus\n  **fountain XOR: 3.4 KB/packet at d ≤ 64 (D25) = 0.8 MB/s** at this geometry's\n  **450 packets/s** (15 tiles × 2 packets/tile × 15 fps, using the R2 nominal rung) —\n  negligible, but only because of the cap. Uncapped it is 6.1 MB/s\n  at K = 768, and was 91.8 MB/s at the old K = 16,384.\n\nBecause indices derive from a PRNG (D7), the sender is **stateless**: frame *N* generates\ndirectly without replaying 1…*N*−1. That is what makes resume and repair nearly free.\n\n**Implementation:** worker generator → ring buffer (depth 3) → main thread paints via\n`rAF`. Deeper buffering is wasted memory (I7).\n\n#### 6.3.2 Shape the code region to the CAMERA, not the screen\n\nMeasured, and worth ~4–5× on its own. The receiver's camera has a fixed aspect and a fixed\npixel count; the sender's screen has a different one. What matters is **camera px per module**\n(§2), and that is set by how much of the capture the code region fills.\n\nA 1920×1080 landscape code region imaged by a portrait 1080×1920 capture yields **M = 0.5625** —\nso 4 screen px/module is only 2.25 camera px/module, below the cliff. Rendering the *same*\npayload into a **portrait-shaped region** inverts this:\n\n| Code region on screen | M | Camera px/module @ 2 screen px | Tiles | QR cap/frame | Payload/frame |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 1920×1080 (naive: fill the screen) | 0.56 | 1.13 — **far below cliff** | 15 | 8.8 KB | 7.5 KB |\n| 1080×1080 square | 1.00 | 2.00 — below cliff | 9 | 5.3 KB | 4.5 KB |\n| **540×960 portrait** | **2.00** | **4.00 — above cliff** | 15 | **8.8 KB** | **7.5 KB** |\n\nSame tile count and same bytes per frame as the naive layout, but *above* the cliff instead of\nbelow it — so yield goes from roughly a fifth to near-total. **The sender MUST size the code\nregion to the receiver's capture aspect, not to its own display.** Since there is no\nback-channel, it cannot know that aspect: expose it as a user-visible setting (portrait /\nlandscape receiver) **defaulting to portrait, which is how phones are held — and portrait is\na fully supported mode, not a degraded one.** The 540×960 portrait region above clears the\ncliff (4.00 camera px/module) at the *same* 7.5 KB/frame payload as the naive landscape\nlayout. **Phase 3's ≥ 20 KB/s gate MUST pass with the receiver held portrait, unaided** —\nthat is the default, unassisted case, not a stretch goal.\n\n**Packets-per-tile basis.** The R2 nominal rung (v16-L, 60% of tiles in steady state per D18a)\ncarries **2 packets per tile**. Each packet is 269 B (13-byte header + 256 B payload), so\n2 packets = 538 B per tile, which fits within v16-L's 586 B capacity. The **user-visible payload**\nis 15 tiles × 2 packets/tile × 256 B = **7,680 B/frame ≈ 7.5 KB/frame**, matching the table\nabove (per §13.2, all throughput figures quote user-visible bytes, not wire bytes). The **8.8 KB/frame\nQR capacity** is 15 tiles × 586 B (v16-L capacity). At 15 fps, this geometry delivers\n**7.5 KB × 15 fps = 112.5 KB/s payload rate** (or ~113 KB/s) before fountain overhead\nand erasure loss.\n\n**Two routes to the same M; landscape is a free bonus, not a requirement.** Physically holding\nthe receiver in landscape puts the screen's long axis on the camera's long axis — **1.78×,\nfree, and it does not require halving screen px/module the way the portrait-region layout\ndoes** — so it is worth *offering* to a user willing to turn the phone. But the app MUST NOT\ndepend on the user doing so: the sender-side portrait region (above) is the primary,\nalways-on path, and landscape is strictly an optional upgrade for extra margin on top of it.\n\nVerified negative: forcing the receiver's *OS* orientation does not help — sensor mapping\nfollows the device body, not the UI. Since portrait is the supported default, this mostly\ndoesn't matter; it only matters for the optional landscape upgrade, which needs a *physical*\nturn (§11 `E-ORIENTATION`, reframed below as a tip, not a requirement).\n\n### 6.4 Receiver pipeline\n\n```\ngetUserMedia ──► exposureCompensation:min (D14) ──► measure real fps (rVFC, ~1 s)\n      │\n      └──► requestVideoFrameCallback ──► MediaStreamTrackProcessor*\n                                                │\n                              ROI crop (conditional — see §6.4)\n                                                │\n                              ┌─────────────────┴──── Worker pool ────┐\n                              ▼                                       ▼\n                      zxing readBarcodes                     [Stage 2: split\n                      (all symbols, .bytes)                   R/G/B, stretch, ×3]\n                              │\n                    header parse ──► fcrc ──► streamId lock ──► route by blockIndex\n                              │                                        │\n                     beacon? This is *not* the whole-receiver figure; see I6a/I6b in §5.\n\nThree rules that are cheap to implement and expensive to omit:\n\n- **Measure fps, never trust it.** `getSettings()` reports 30/60 while the camera\n  delivers 15.\n- **Crop to ROI before decoding — but the 9× is conditional.** Measured 8.6× (56.9 → 6.6 ms)\n  *when the code occupies part of the frame*.
